items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to reimbursement for
special transportation services
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S4770

SPONSOR: SALAZAR
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the social services law, in relation
to reimbursement for special transportation services

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This legislation aims at improving the School Supportive Health Services
Program by ensuring that all possible available federal funds that cover
transportation needs for children with handicaps are pursued.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1: Section 368-d of the social services law is amended by adding
a new subdivision 7 to read as follows: The commissioner shall, begin-
ning upon the effective date of this subdivision and on an ongoing basis
thereafter, review whether current state rules, regulations, policy,
billing guidelines and amendments under the state plan for medical
assistance concerning Medicaid reimbursement for special transportation
services, which are furnished by school districts to children with
handicapping conditions, or such children suspected of having handicap-
ping conditions, receiving medical care and services that qualify for
reimbursement under this title, are more restrictive than required by
federal law, regulations, or policy.

The commissioner shall take all practicable steps to ensure that any
necessary changes are made to state rules, regulations, policy, and
billing guidelines and submit any necessary proposed state plan amend-
ments to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, to ensure
receipt of all available federal financial participation under Title
Nineteen of the federal Social Security Act for special transportation
services furnished by school districts to children with handicapping
conditions or such children suspected of having handicapping conditions.

This section outlines responsibilities of commissioner in securing
available federal funding for the purposes of serving children with
handicapping conditions, including considering best practice policies in
other states, and consultation with school district and school offi-
cials.

Section 2: Section 368-e of the Social Services Law is amended by adding
a new subdivision 6 that reads as amendment to Section 368-d subdivision
7 above.

Section 3: This section shall take effect immediately.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

New York State takes a very restrictive interpretation of federal
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Service (CMS) requirements for
specialized transportation claiming federal guidelines indicate that if
a Medicaid eligible child requires transportation in a vehicle adapted
for the child's disability and that medical need is listed on the
child's IEP, the transportation service is claimable.

However, federal guidelines do not outline a specific definition of an
adapted vehicle. While definitions for "special adapted vehicles" vary
amongst states, New York State has the most restrictive definition.
Guidance from NYS DOH limits reimbursement only to vehicles with phys-
ical adaptations such as a wheelchair ramp, lift or tinted window.

New Jersey, Virginia, Pennsylvania and Massachusetts are a few examples
of states that have interpreted federal CMS guidelines on transportation
more broadly than New York State allowing them to claim reimbursement at
higher amounts to transport these children.

The New York City Department of Education (DOE) estimates there are
approximately 25,000 students served with a requirement for special
transportation and at least one accommodation or adaptation, including:

* Safety restraints
* Medical equipment/devices (including oxygen tanks)
* Nursing services
* Climate control, ultraviolet shield
* Tinted windows
* Reduced size vehicles, and limited travel time Solution

New York City is requesting that New York State DOH revise its
policy/guidance to expand the scope of claimable adaptations in accord-
ance with federal CMS guidelines, and to include but not be limited to:
Safety restraints, medical equipment, paraprofessional or nursing
services, smaller vehicle size, alternative vehicle routing and climate
control.

This action allows DOE to maximize federal Medicaid funding available
for these services under the School Supportive Health Services Program.

 
EXISTING LAW:

New Legislation

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

None. Will actually increase federal funds to New York City to cover
costs of transporting children with handicapping conditions.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This section shall take effect immediately.

summary: Enables the commissioner of social services to review state plans which provide for special transportation services for children and pre-school children to ensure that state policies are not more restrictive than policies at the federal level.
title: Relates to enabling the commissioner of social services to review state plans for special transportation services for children

items.memoText:
VETO MESSAGE - No. 272
 
TO THE SENATE:
 
I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bill:
 
Senate Bill Number 4770-A, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to reimburse-
      ment for special transportation services"
 
    NOT APPROVED
 
  This bill would require the Department  of  Health  ("Department")  to
review all state Medicaid rules, regulations, policy, billing guidelines
and  state  plan  amendments  for medical care services that provide for
special transportation services for children and pre-school children  to
ensure  that  state  policies  are not more restrictive than required by
federal law, regulations or policies.  The bill would also  require  the
Commissioner  to  take  all  steps  to ensure the state is receiving all
available federal financial  participation  for  special  transportation
services furnished by school districts.
 
  I directed the Department to engage the Canters for Medicare and Medi-
caid Services on a state plan amendment and policy guidelines for school
supportive  health services and the Department has been advised that the
state's  current  policies  are  fully  compliant  with  federal  rules.
Further,  as part of the FY 2017 Enacted Budget, New York City agreed to
establish a plan that would identify $55 million  in  state  savings  in
their  school  supportive  health  services program. The City has yet to
establish such plan.
 
  While ensuring the state has access to maximized federal resources  is
a laudable effort, New York City should be equally focused on finalizing
their  plan to adhere with the FY 2017 Enacted Budget agreement.  As the
bill is currently drafted, it would duplicate the efforts  that  Depart-
ment  has already made with respect to this effort. Faced with the pros-
pect that the city of New York is instead looking to Centers  for  Medi-
care  and  Medicaid  Services  for  further savings to aid them in their
effort to identify funds for such savings, the bill is  simply  shifting
the  burden to identify savings to the state at significant cost. I urge
the city of New York to identify their savings as soon as possible.  For
these foregoing reasons, I must veto the bill.
 
  The bill is disapproved.                    (signed) ANDREW M. CUOMO
 
                               __________
